text: Where does the name of God come from?
Hey everybody, I'm Dan McClellan. I'm a
scholar of the Bible and religion. And
according to the Hebrew Bible, the
divine name is spelled Yod Heh Vav Heh
or YHWH, and this is known as the
Tetragrammaton, which is Greek for the
four letters. But there are other
spellings in the Bible as well, such as
just Yod Heh or Yod Heh Vav. Now many of
y'all know that as an accommodation to
the Jewish members of my audience, I do
not use the most commonly accepted
reconstruction of the pronunciation of
the divine name. Instead, I use the
substitution Adonai, which is a special
form of the Hebrew word for Lord.
But the Tetragrammaton is either based
on a verb or based on a noun. And while
I want to discuss a couple of theories
that understand it to be based on a
noun, I think the majority view is that
it is based on a verb. And specifically,
the verbal root hayah. This is after all
the folk etymology that we find in
Exodus 3, where God tells Moses to tell
the Israelites that ehyeh asher ehyeh
sent him, which would be I am what I am
or I will be what I will be. So, there's
a long-standing association of name with
the verbal root hayah. And I think for a
long time, the leading theory was that
it was actually a causative form of that
verbal root. So, the Tetragrammaton
would mean he creates or causes to be.
And this theory usually also suggests
that the divine name was originally part
of a longer compound sentence name,
Adonai El. And so God's name was
originally El creates. And so the name
would have reference to the creator
status of the God of Israel. But there
are other theories as well that
understand it as a noun. For instance,
there's a fascinating discussion in this
volume from a few years ago by Josef
Tropper, which is an English translation
of an earlier German article that
suggests the original spelling was just
Yod Heh Vav, and that the final Heh is
actually lectio difficilior indicating
the absolutive state. And this would
match the inscriptional spellings of,
for instance, the name Asher that we
find at Kuntillet Ajrud. But this theory
has not
found widespread acceptance. Another
fascinating theory, which I think was
represented very well in Daniel
Fleming's recent book, suggests that it
is based on the name of a people or the
name of a place. And this goes to some
14th and 13th century Egyptian
inscriptions that long predate the
earliest occurrence of the divine name
in a Northwest Semitic language. And we
find there a reference to nomadic groups
known as Shasu, and one of them is the
Shasu of the land, and then the Egyptian
spells out YHW and then a glottal stop.
And a lot of scholars think this is a
form of the divine name before it was
actually a divine name, but was the name
of a people group or the name of the
land that they occupied.
And according to this theory, this
nomadic group migrated into the central
or northern hill country, bringing with
them their patron deity, who is named
after the land or the people, and that
then entered the Israelite pantheon as a
second-tier deity whose name was the
Tetragrammaton. And then later on, that
deity would be conflated with the
Northwest Semitic high deity El, who
preexisted the arrival of the Shasu
people into that territory. I think this
is a fascinating theory that merits a
lot more investigation. But for the time
being, the most common theory is that
Adonai, the Tetragrammaton, is based
somehow on the verbal root hayah, which
means to be or to become. And the fit
for this video
is Wolverine.
